transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, yeah… thanks. I guess what finally pushed me to make an appointment is that I keep making these small mistakes in things I turn in, and they’re not huge in the sense that, like, nobody’s getting hurt, but they’re embarrassing and they make me look careless.

Like I’ll submit an application or send over research notes, and later I’ll realize I mislabeled something — for example, an artwork date — or I skipped a question that I really thought I had answered. And the frustrating part is I usually do think I’ve checked it. I’ll look it over and feel like, okay, this is fine, and then afterward there’s some obvious little error sitting there. It’s happened enough that I’m starting to worry people think I just don’t care, when I actually do care a lot.

Would you say you've struggled with this kind of overlooking details or making small mistakes for as long as you can remember, even back in school, or is this something that's really only been happening recently?

Yeah, no, it’s definitely not just recent. I mean, it feels more noticeable now because the stakes are higher and I’m the one responsible for catching it, but when I think back, this was there even in elementary school.

I remember teachers writing things on report cards or comments like, basically, that I had good ideas or understood the material, but then I’d forget to turn in worksheets, or I’d lose the instructions for an assignment, or I’d miss these little details that other kids seemed to just… notice. And my parents had to check my backpack almost every night, because otherwise there’d be some crumpled worksheet I forgot existed, or something I was supposed to bring back to school that just never made it out of my bag.

So I don’t think it came out of nowhere. It’s more like it’s the same pattern, just now there isn’t a teacher or my parents catching it before it causes a problem.

Aside from the attention and organization issues, do you notice things like feeling restless, fidgeting, having trouble sitting still, or acting impulsively—like blurting things out or interrupting others—either now or when you were a kid?

I’m not sure I’d describe myself as, like, physically restless in a big obvious way. The thing I do notice, though, is that I can talk too much once I get going.

It happens most in seminars or gallery conversations, especially if it’s a topic I’m excited about or I feel like I’ve finally connected an idea in my head. I’ll start explaining it, and then I sort of keep adding context and examples because I’m trying to be clear, but afterward I realize I basically took up the whole space. Like, I’ll think back and realize someone else was about to respond, or there was a natural pause where I could have stopped, and I just… didn’t. I kept going.

It’s not that I mean to interrupt or dominate, exactly. In the moment it feels like I’m just following the thought to the end, but then later I feel embarrassed because I realize I barely left room for anyone else to say anything.

Would you say these attention slips and talking-too-much moments cause noticeable problems for you in more than one area of your life—like at work, at home, and in your relationships—or is it mostly limited to one setting?

Yeah, it’s more than one setting. I mean, the biggest consequences show up around school or applications or work-type things, because that’s where there’s a deadline and someone can actually see the mistake. I’ve submitted things late because I underestimated how long it would take me to pull the final pieces together, or because I thought I was basically done and then realized I’d missed some requirement.

And I’ve missed a couple of application deadlines, which felt awful because they weren’t things I didn’t care about. They were things I really did want to do, and I just didn’t manage the follow-through well enough. One of my mentors actually told me pretty directly that my follow-through is starting to hurt opportunities I should be ready for, and that was kind of hard to hear because I know they’re right.

At home or socially it’s maybe less formal, but it still shows up in the sense that I’ll have to go back and fix things or apologize for not getting something done when I said I would. But the place where it feels most noticeable is definitely with deadlines, applications, and people relying on me to be thorough.

Have you been experiencing any ongoing feelings of sadness, low motivation, or excessive worry/anxiety that might be affecting your concentration, or does the trouble focusing happen even when your mood and anxiety levels feel normal?

I’m not totally sure how to separate all of that out, honestly. I mean, I do get stressed when I’m behind or when I realize I’ve missed something, but that feels more like a reaction to the mess I’m already in, if that makes sense.

I wouldn’t say there’s some constant sadness or anxiety that explains it, at least not that I’ve noticed. The focusing problems happen even when I’m in a basically okay mood, or when I’m not especially worried about anything. Like, I can be having a normal day and still sit down to do something and somehow drift off, miss a step, or avoid starting until way too late.

So… I guess my answer is that mood and anxiety can make it worse sometimes, especially once I’m already stressed about consequences, but the trouble focusing doesn’t seem to only happen because I’m sad or anxious. It’s there even when I feel pretty normal.
Thinking back to before you were about 12 years old, were you already showing several of these attention and organization difficulties at that time, not just occasionally but as a regular pattern?

Yeah, I think so. I mean, I don’t remember it as clearly as my parents probably do, but from what I do remember—and from old report cards and comments—it was already kind of a pattern in elementary school.

Teachers would say things like I had good ideas, or that I understood the material when I actually did the work, but then there’d be these notes about me not turning in worksheets, or losing the instructions, or missing small details. And it wasn’t like I was trying to be difficult. I’d do part of something and then somehow the sheet wouldn’t make it back into the folder, or I’d forget there was a second side, or I’d bring home the wrong paper.

My parents had to check my backpack basically every night for a while, because otherwise things would just disappear into it. Like permission slips, worksheets, instructions from the teacher—stuff that probably looked simple from the outside, but I just wasn’t reliably keeping track of it. So yes, I’d say it was there before middle school, not just once in a while.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports a longstanding, pervasive pattern of inattentive symptoms (careless mistakes, losing/forgetting materials, poor follow-through, difficulty sustaining attention on tasks) beginning before age 12 and persisting into adulthood, corroborated by childhood teacher/parent reports. Mild impulsivity (excessive talking, difficulty yielding conversational turns) is present but less prominent than inattentive symptoms. Symptoms occur across multiple settings (school/work, home, relationships) and cause functional impairment (missed deadlines, jeopardized opportunities). Mood and anxiety symptoms are secondary/reactive rather than primary, and attentional difficulties persist independent of mood state, making ADHD the best-fitting diagnosis over an anxiety or mood disorder.
